$comment: THE deployed-source invoke contract, as data. One file, three implementations.
`src/features/hosting/source-invoke.ts` is the prose contract; this is the
executable one. Three separate programs claim to speak it and only one of them
can be redeployed at will:
1. `src/features/hosting/source-shim.mjs` — bundled into every deployed
source. Runs this file in `test/unit/features/hosting/source-shim.test.ts`.
2. `@ontrove/sdk`'s `createSourceWorker` — not written yet. It must run this
file as its own gate before it is published, not merely be read against it.
3. `trove-macos/Runtime/runner.js` — ships INSIDE AN INSTALLED BINARY with no
forced update. A contract change that this file does not catch reaches
users as a silently broken sync on a build nobody can recall.
That third one is the reason the contract is a fixture rather than a paragraph.
The Mac runner cannot be fixed retroactively, so the only defence is a shared
artefact both sides execute: whichever side changes, the other side's run of
this file goes red in CI first.
Every case carries a `why`. A case with no stated failure is a case nobody can
safely delete, and this file is read by people in other repositories who have
no access to the conversation that produced it.
`{"$repeat": {"unit": "x", "times": N}}` expands to a string of N units.
It is how a 64 KB cursor and a 4 MiB body fit in a file a human can read.
Asserted against the exported constants, so a limit cannot move without this
file — the copy other repositories read — moving in the same commit.

route.name: POST /sync is the whole surface
route.why: One route, one shape. Anything else is not the contract.

route.name: a path ENDING in /sync is accepted
route.why: The dispatch host is meaningless and a wrapper may mount the worker under a prefix. Suffix matching, not equality — an implementation that compares the whole pathname rejects requests the shim accepts.

route.name: GET is not a sync
route.why: A sync is not idempotent and must never be reachable by a bare browser fetch or a warm-up prober.

route.name: another path is not a sync
route.why: There is no second route to grow into. An isolate holds no Trove capability, so any other path answering anything is a surface that should not exist.

context.name: config, credentials and cursor reach the adapter unchanged
context.why: An adapter must behave identically under every runtime. Anything reshaped here is a bug that only appears once a source is deployed.

context.name: a wire null cursor becomes undefined
context.why: JSON has no undefined, so a first run arrives as null. Adapters test `if (!ctx.cursor)` — but one that tests `ctx.cursor === undefined` would treat null as a real cursor and try to resume from it.

context.name: a missing config or credentials becomes an empty object
context.why: A source declaring no credentials still has adapters that read `ctx.credentials.FOO`. Undefined there is a TypeError at the top of every such sync.

context.name: a typed watermark cursor arrives byte-identical
context.why: `src/features/ingest/watermark.ts` and the adapter's own writer describe the SAME object, not merely the same bytes — `idSet.max` is the retention CAP (a count), not the highest id. A runtime that re-shaped the cursor in transit would make the two types disagree in a way no test on either side could see.

context.name: deadlineMs sets an absolute deadline
context.why: `ctx.deadline` is an epoch millisecond, not a duration. An adapter that loops until `Date.now() < ctx.deadline` runs forever against a duration and is killed mid-write.

context.name: a missing deadlineMs falls back to the declared default
context.why: A runner that forgets the field must not hand the adapter NaN, which makes every deadline comparison false and every bounded loop unbounded.

context.name: log, progress and fetch exist; cache does not
context.why: `cache` is a KV-backed cross-run scratchpad and a deployed isolate holds no Trove capability at all (docs/32 D1). Adapters already guard `if (!ctx.cache) return` because the Mac runtime does not always supply one — so its absence is degradation they were written for. `progress` must still be callable (a no-op is fine): there is no channel back mid-invocation, but an adapter that calls it must not crash.

roundTrip.name: documents and a cursor
roundTrip.why: The ordinary successful round: what the adapter returned, plus the logs it wrote, in the runner's vocabulary.

roundTrip.name: an empty run
roundTrip.why: Nothing new is the normal answer for most syncs and must not be mistaken for a failure.

roundTrip.name: an adapter that returns nothing at all
roundTrip.why: Adapters that only ever no-op sometimes fall off the end of the function. That is an empty run, not a malformed response — failing it would break working sources over a style detail.

roundTrip.name: a null cursor means KEEP THE PRIOR ONE, end to end
roundTrip.why: THE case. A shim writing `cursor: ctx.cursor ?? null` emits null on every first run, so null crosses the wire constantly. Reading it as 'clear the cursor' blanks the watermark and re-fetches the whole feed next sync — a bill on a metered source, a silent duplicate ingest on any of them. Null is allowed ON the wire and dropped by the reader; an adapter that really wants to restart says so by resetting the feed cursor, which is an operator action with a name. Emitting `cursor: null` and omitting the key are the SAME statement, because the reader drops null either way — so both are conformant here, and an implementation is not wrong for choosing the tidier one.

roundTrip.name: omitted optional fields stay omitted
roundTrip.why: An absent cursor and an explicit null both mean 'keep the prior one', but only absence may be invented by the runtime. Emitting `cursor: undefined` as `cursor: null` would be harmless; emitting `stats: {}` or `feedName: ''` would overwrite a feed's real name with nothing.

roundTrip.name: feedName and feedUrl cross the boundary
roundTrip.why: docs/32 D1 sketches only {documents, cursor, stats, logs}. Dropping these makes every deployed feed show a URL instead of a name, and leaves a permanently moved feed unable to say where it went — a runtime that is quietly worse in ways nobody attributes to the runtime.

roundTrip.name: a typed watermark survives the return trip verbatim
roundTrip.why: The cursor an adapter returns is handed straight back as `ctx.cursor` next run. If either leg re-shapes it — stringifying it, dropping `max`, renaming a field — the feed silently resumes from the wrong place.

roundTrip.name: logs are buffered, levelled, and stringify their parts
roundTrip.why: There is no line streaming across the invoke boundary, so the transcript is whatever came back in this array. A level prefix is what makes a failed run readable; a runtime that dropped non-string parts would silently lose the counts adapters log.

roundTrip.name: a thrown adapter is a 500 carrying its message and its logs
roundTrip.why: The dangerous alternative is to catch and return {documents: []}, which reads to the runner as 'nothing new' — the cursor then advances past everything the adapter failed to fetch and the loss is permanent and invisible. The logs ride along because a failing run is exactly when the narration is worth reading.

response.name: an opaque string cursor is accepted verbatim
response.why: The Mac runner normalises every cursor to a JSON STRING before it returns it, because the host stores an opaque string. The reader must not insist on an object, and must not helpfully parse it — either would make one of the two live runtimes wrong about what it just stored.

response.name: unknown top-level fields are ignored, not rejected
response.why: The Mac runner returns `cookies` alongside the result, and it ships in a binary that cannot be recalled. Rejecting an unrecognised field would turn any future addition on either side into a hard failure for every installed build; the reader keeps only what it knows.

response.name: a document keeps every field the ingest path understands
response.why: The reader validates shape and forwards the document whole. Whitelisting fields here would silently drop metadata, tags and capture_only — the marks an adapter writes precisely because nothing downstream can re-derive them.

response.name: an audio_url document needs no text
response.why: A podcast episode's body is produced by transcription on the server. Demanding text here would reject every audio source.

response.name: a file_url document needs no text
response.why: The server downloads, retains and extracts the file. Same reasoning as audio: the body arrives later.

response.name: a cursor exactly at the cap is accepted
response.why: The limit is a ceiling, not a target. Pinning the boundary inclusive stops an implementation rejecting the largest legal cursor over an off-by-one — a failure that would only show up on the one source with the biggest id set.

response.name: one byte over the cursor cap is refused
response.why: The cursor lands in the tenant's own SQLite shard, whose space IS the user's primary data. An adapter that stuffed a page of HTML into its cursor would be spending the user's storage on its own bookkeeping.

response.name: a document with no ingestible body is refused
response.why: A title with no text, audio_url or file_url ingests as a successful empty document — indistinguishable downstream from a real one that happens to be short.

response.name: the offending document is named by index
response.why: The adapter's author has to find it, and they cannot be asked what they meant.

response.name: one bad document fails the WHOLE response
response.why: The tempting behaviour is to drop the bad one and keep the rest. That turns an adapter bug into a silently short run AND advances the cursor past what was dropped, so the loss is permanent and nothing downstream ever reports it.

response.name: a document with no id is refused
response.why: The id is the external key dedupe hangs off. Without it every run re-ingests the same item as new.

response.name: stats must be an object
response.why: An array passes a naive typeof check and then reads as `{0: ...}` wherever stats is spread.

response.name: feedName must be a string
response.why: It becomes a feed's displayed label. A number here renames the feed to a number.

response.name: feedUrl must be a string
response.why: It becomes a fetch target. Shape is checked here; the write-time URL policy every hand-typed config value gets is applied by the seam, not by this reader.

response.name: a response that is not an object is refused
response.why: A proxy that answers with a bare JSON string is not an isolate answering the contract.

response.name: a response with no documents array is refused
response.why: `documents` is the only required field. Defaulting it to [] would let a crashed adapter read as a successful empty sync.

response.name: non-string log lines are dropped, not fatal
response.why: Logs are diagnostics, not data. A bad line is worth ignoring; a bad DOCUMENT is not — that is the distinction the whole reader is drawing.

http.name: a good 200 is read
http.why: The baseline the rest of the cases are deviations from.

http.name: a non-2xx fails loudly, carrying the isolate's own words
http.why: The adapter author debugs from this line, so the body has to survive into the message.

http.name: an oversized body is refused by its DECLARED length, before parsing
http.why: Parsing is where an oversized response does its damage: a 400 MiB body exhausts the isolate's 128 MiB long before any length check on the parsed value could run.

http.name: an oversized body that under-declared its length is still refused
http.why: content-length is the isolate's claim, not a fact. The raw bytes are checked too.

http.name: invalid JSON reports enough of the body to diagnose it
http.why: The usual cause is an HTML error page from something in front of the isolate, and the first 200 characters say which thing.

http.name: a 500 in the shim's shape lifts its logs onto the error
http.why: Folding them into the message left the adapter's own account of itself as a JSON blob inside a sentence — legible to nobody, at the exact moment someone is reading. The runner replays these as ordinary transcript lines.

http.name: a 500 that is not the shim's shape still reports the failure
http.why: A crash before the handler, a proxy error page, an empty body: the log lift must never become the reason a failure goes unreported.

http.name: an empty 500 body still reports the failure
http.why: Same reasoning, and the case a naive JSON.parse of the body would throw on.

http.name: only string log lines are lifted off a failure
http.why: The error path runs while handling a failure; a surprise in the logs must not replace the failure being reported.
